Then a young pilot, Altman had just gotten back from a 7½-month tour onboard an aircraft carrier when he got the "Top Gun" call from his commanding officer. "The skipper of our squadron picked four guys he thought he could trust to have this kind of carte blanche to break the rules a little bit," Altman said. That included a scene in which a brazen Navy pilot buzzes the base's control tower. That would never happen in real life, Altman said. The movie features Cruise as a young naval aviator, Pete "Maverick" Mitchell, selected to attend fighter-pilot training school at the then-Miramar Naval Station north of San Diego. To prepare for the film, Cruise flew in the backseat of an F-14 several times, including once with Altman. "The actors were all pretty easy to get along with. Tom Cruise, for example, was very motivated," recalled Altman, who is making his fourth trip into space this week. "He enjoyed flying. He listened to what we told him and became a pilot himself after that." Altman is not one to brag about his flying in "Top Gun." The U.S. space agency, NASA, doesn't mention his film heroics, either. But Altman is in one of the movie's most memorable scenes. While flying upside down, inverted, Altman gives an obscene gesture to the pilot of an enemy plane. "They said go ahead and gesture at the other airplane," said Altman, 49, with a smile. "So when you're looking at the scene where he's communicating with the Russian, or the bad-guy pilots in the movie, that would be my finger." But the flying scenes with the actors didn't all work out as director Tony Scott had hoped. "The director had to pay $7,600 an hour to rent an airplane," Altman recalled. "But after a week of spending that much money on the airplanes, he decided he couldn't use the footage. The actors all looked a little green, he said." Altman and the other pilots earned $23 a day for their trouble. But his biggest disappointment was not getting to see the film as soon as it was released. He and the other pilots were invited to a preview screening, but a commanding officer would not let them go. And by the time the movie hit theaters, Altman was busy. He was overseas, on another seven-month tour of duty.

# Kennedy Space Center: Gateway to the Stars

The Kennedy Space Center, located on Merritt Island, Florida, stands as one of the most significant facilities in the history of human spaceflight. Established by NASA in 1962, it has served as the primary launch site for the United States space program for over six decades.

## A Storied History

Named after President John F. Kennedy, whose 1961 challenge to land a man on the Moon before the decade's end galvanized the nation's space ambitions, the center became the operational heart of America's most ambitious space endeavors. It was from this location that the Apollo missions launched, culminating in the historic Apollo 11 mission that brought Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to the lunar surface in July 1969.

## Evolution Through the Decades

Following the Apollo era, Kennedy Space Center adapted to new challenges. The site became home to the Space Shuttle program, launching all 135 shuttle missions between 1981 and 2011. This program pushed the boundaries of reusable spacecraft technology and enabled the construction of the International Space Station.

## The Modern Era

Today, Kennedy Space Center continues to evolve as a hub for both governmental and commercial spaceflight. It now hosts launches from private companies like SpaceX and Boeing, reflecting the changing landscape of space exploration. The center has embraced partnerships with commercial entities while maintaining its role in NASA's deep space ambitions, including the Artemis program aimed at returning humans to the Moon and eventually reaching Mars.

## A Center for Innovation and Education

Beyond its launch operations, Kennedy Space Center serves as an educational and cultural landmark. Its visitor complex attracts millions of tourists annually, offering exhibits on space history, rocket launches, and astronaut training experiences. The center plays a vital role in inspiring future generations of scientists, engineers, and explorers.

## Conclusion

Kennedy Space Center remains a symbol of human ingenuity and our persistent drive to explore beyond our home planet. As commercial spaceflight expands and new missions to the Moon and Mars take shape, this historic site continues to serve as a crucial launching point for humanity's continued journey into the cosmos.

"It's funny how life works," Reynolds said in an interview at Johnson Space Center. "Back then, I was just a young Navy pilot trying not to black out during a 7-G turn. I never imagined that experience would eventually lead me to space."

"Mark has this rare ability to stay composed under pressure," said fellow astronaut Dr. Elena Cho, who will join Reynolds on the upcoming mission. "Whether it's a docking maneuver or an in-flight emergency simulation, his instincts are incredible. Now I understand why."

# From Hollywood Skies to Orbital Heights: Astronaut Reflects on Flying for Tom Cruise

**HOUSTON** — In a career that reads like a Hollywood script itself, veteran astronaut Colonel Mark Reeves has done something few people on Earth can claim: he's piloted aircraft for a Tom Cruise production *and* commanded a space shuttle mission. We sat down with Reeves to discuss the surprising parallels—and stark differences—between flying for the silver screen and flying for NASA.

**Q: Let's start from the beginning. How did you end up flying for a Tom Cruise film?**

Reeves laughs. "Back in the late '90s, before I joined the astronaut corps, I was an active-duty test pilot. The production needed experienced pilots who could fly precision aerobatic sequences for the cameras—tight formations, specific angles, repeatable maneuvers. It wasn't combat flying, but it required an insane level of control. Tom actually flew alongside us in some sequences. The guy is a genuine aviation enthusiast—he wasn't just an actor sitting in a mock-up."

**Q: What was that experience like compared to your astronaut training?**

"Honestly, they scratch different itches. Film flying is about *performance*—you're hitting marks in three-dimensional space while a camera plane tracks you, and the director wants specific lighting, specific banking angles. It's choreography. You're an artist as much as a pilot.

Space shuttle piloting is about *precision under irreversible consequence*. There's no 'cut, let's try that again.' When you're guiding 100 tons of orbiter through re-entry at Mach 25, descending like a glider with zero engine power, you get exactly one shot. That changes your entire relationship with the controls."

**Q: Did the film work actually help prepare you in any way?**

"More than people would guess. Formation flying teaches spatial awareness and muscle memory under pressure that translates directly to orbital rendezvous and docking. When you're bringing the shuttle within inches of the International Space Station, closing at fractions of a foot per second, that same disciplined, unhurried hand you develop doing tight formation passes for a camera—it's there. You've trained your body not to overcorrect.

Also, both jobs taught me to perform complex tasks while people are watching intensely and expecting perfection. In film, it's a director and producers. In spaceflight, it's mission control, the public, and frankly, history."

**Q: Any moment during your shuttle missions where you thought back to the movie set?**

"Actually, yes. During my final approach and landing at Edwards, I had this fleeting thought: this is the ultimate one-take scene. No stunt double, no digital effects, no do-overs. Tom used to talk about wanting audiences to feel real speed, real stakes. I remember thinking, 'This is about as real as it gets.'"

**Q: Final thoughts on the comparison?**

"People assume Hollywood flying is the 'fake' version and NASA flying is the 'real' version, and there's truth to that hierarchy. But both demand total command of your aircraft and total command of your fear. The main difference is that in the movies, if I mess up, we reshoot. In space, the film keeps rolling whether you're ready or not."

Reeves is set to speak at an upcoming aerospace symposium about the surprising crossover skills between cinematic aviation and human spaceflight—a talk he's simply titled: *"No Second Takes."*

"In both cases, you're managing extreme risk while a hundred things are happening at once, and you have to trust your training completely."

## Flying for the Cameras

Harrison, then a young Navy lieutenant stationed at Naval Air Station Miramar, was selected as one of a handful of active-duty pilots to fly precision maneuvers for the film's now-iconic aerial sequences.

"We'd fly formations so tight you could see the sweat on the other pilot's face," Harrison recalled, laughing. "Tony Scott, the director, wanted shots that looked impossible. Half our job was figuring out how to make something look dangerous while staying within the safety margins the Navy demanded."

The work required extraordinary precision — flying inverted, executing high-G maneuvers, and repeating complex sequences multiple times for different camera angles, all while coordinating with camera planes and ground crews.

"There's a scene where two Tomcats pass canopy-to-canopy," Harrison said. "We rehearsed that maneuver for days. It's one thing to do something once under adrenaline. It's another to do it precisely, on command, take after take."

## From Cockpit to Capsule

Harrison says the discipline of stunt flying — hitting exact marks, communicating constantly with a team, and staying calm under pressure — became foundational when he transitioned to NASA's astronaut corps in the early 1990s.

"When I was commanding STS-118, there were moments during ascent where things happened fast, and I found myself drawing on that same mental framework," he said. "Stay calm. Trust the checklist. Trust your crew."

Harrison went on to command two shuttle missions before retiring from NASA in 2011, logging more than 40 days in space.

## A Legacy Beyond the Screen

While "Top Gun" became a cultural phenomenon — famously boosting Navy recruitment numbers in the years following its release — Harrison says few people realize how many of the film's pilots went on to distinguished careers, including several who, like him, later became astronauts.

"We weren't actors," he said. "We were just doing our jobs, and it happened that our jobs looked good on camera."

With "Top Gun: Maverick" reviving interest in naval aviation once again, Harrison says he's been fielding more questions than ever about those early days above the California coastline.

"It's strange to think a movie I flew stunts for as a 20-something lieutenant would still be part of my story decades later," he said. "But I suppose that's fitting — flying's always been about looking forward while making peace with where you've been."

Harrison, now 68, continues to speak to students about STEM careers, often opening his talks with a clip from the film before revealing his own connection to it.

"I tell kids: the sky was never the limit," he said. "It was just the beginning."
